scenes.heading: Will the reaction actually go? Three steps to the answer.
scenes.body: IQ3 is the climax of the module. To decide whether a reaction is spontaneous, you walk a ladder: predict ΔS, calculate ΔS°, then combine with ΔH° via Gibbs. One process, three skills.

bullets.text: Step 1: predict ΔS sign from gas moles (L11).
Step 2: calculate ΔS° from a table (L12).
Step 3: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° → sign decides (L13).

scenes.callout: Three steps from disorder prediction to a spontaneity answer.
scenes.caption: ΔS sign → ΔS° value → ΔG°; the IQ3 ladder.

voiceover.text: IQ3 is the climax of the module. To decide whether a reaction is spontaneous, you climb a ladder of three skills. First, predict the sign of delta S by counting gas moles — that's qualitative. Second, calculate delta S zero from a standard entropy table — that's quantitative. Third, combine with delta H zero using the Gibbs equation — delta G zero equals delta H zero minus T delta S zero. The sign of delta G zero is your final answer. Negative means thermodynamically spontaneous.

scenes.heading: The IQ3 decision tree
scenes.body: Read the question and match it to the right skill.

bullets.text: Asked for ΔS sign? → Count gas moles (L11).
Given a table of S° values? → Σ products − Σ reactants (L12).
Asked for spontaneity at given T? → ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° (L13).
Asked for crossover T? → T = ΔH°/ΔS° (L13).

scenes.callout: Sign → S° value → Gibbs. Crossover T = ΔH°/ΔS°.
scenes.caption: Decision tree for IQ3 skills.

voiceover.text: The IQ3 decision tree. Think of it like climbing a three-rung ladder — predict, calculate, then combine. But unlike a physical ladder, you don't always need all three rungs; the question tells you where to start. Asked for the sign of delta S — count gas moles from Lesson eleven. Given a table of standard entropies — apply products minus reactants from Lesson twelve. Asked for spontaneity at a given temperature — use Gibbs from Lesson thirteen, delta G equals delta H minus T delta S. Asked for the crossover temperature — set delta G to zero, so T equals delta H over delta S.

scenes.heading: Walkthrough 1, predict ΔS sign
scenes.question: Predict the sign of ΔS for: (a) 2NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g); (b) CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g); (c) H₂O(l) → H₂O(s).
scenes.coachNote: Count gas moles on each side. State changes matter too.
steps: Known: three equations with different gas-mole changes.
Find: sign of ΔS for each.
(a) Reactant gas = 3 mol; product gas = 2 mol; Δn = −1 → ΔS negative.
(b) Reactant gas = 0; product gas = 1; Δn = +1 → ΔS positive.
Formula: more disorder = more arrangements (gas > liquid > solid).
Substitute: count Δn(gas) for each = (a) 2 − 3 = -1; (b) 1 − 0 = 1; (c) state change l → s.
(c) Liquid → solid → ΔS strongly negative (freezing).
Answer = 3 signs predicted: (a) negative; (b) positive; (c) negative (freezing is ordering).
scenes.caption: Predictions: (a) − (b) + (c) − . Gas moles + state change.

voiceover.text: Walkthrough one — predict three signs. Part a: two NO plus O two giving two NO two — three moles of gas become two. Delta n is minus one, so delta S negative. Part b: calcium carbonate decomposing — zero gas moles becomes one. Delta n plus one, delta S positive. Part c: liquid water freezing to solid ice — that's an ordering process, delta S strongly negative.

scenes.heading: Walkthrough 2, calculate ΔS°
scenes.question: Calculate ΔS° for 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l). Use S°[H₂(g)] = 130.7, S°[O₂(g)] = 205.2, S°[H₂O(l)] = 69.9 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
scenes.coachNote: Sum products − sum reactants, scaled by coefficients. Verify sign against Δn(gas).
steps: Known: S° values; coefficients in the equation.
Find: ΔS° in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
Σ S°(products) = 2 × 69.9 = 139.8 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
Formula: ΔS° = Σ S°(products) − Σ S°(reactants).
Substitute: ΔS° = 139.8 − 466.6.
Check: 3 mol gas → 0 mol gas (liquid), strongly negative, confirmed.
Answer: ΔS° = 326.8 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ decrease (i.e. −326.8 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹).
scenes.caption: ΔS° = 139.8 − 466.6 = −326.8 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

voiceover.text: Walkthrough two — calculate delta S zero for hydrogen combustion to liquid water. Sum products: two times sixty-nine-point-nine, one-thirty-nine-point-eight. Sum reactants: two times one-thirty-point-seven plus one times two-zero-five-point-two, total four-sixty-six-point-six. Delta S zero is one-thirty-nine-point-eight minus four-sixty-six-point-six — minus three hundred and twenty-six-point-eight joules per kelvin per mole. Three gas moles become two liquid moles — strongly negative confirms the qualitative prediction.

scenes.heading: Walkthrough 3, Gibbs spontaneity + crossover T
scenes.question: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g), ΔH° = −92.4 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS° = −198.9 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. (a) ΔG° at 25 °C? (b) Crossover T where ΔG° = 0?
scenes.coachNote: Convert ΔS° to kJ. Convert T to K. Watch the double negative.
steps: Known: ΔH° = −92.4 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔS° = −198.9 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
Find: ΔG° at 25 °C and crossover T.
Convert: T = 298 K, ΔS° = −0.1989 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
Formula: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°.
ΔG°(298 K) = −33.1 kJ mol⁻¹ → forward-favoured in the standard state at 25 °C.
Formula: set ΔG° = 0 → T_cross = ΔH°/ΔS°.
(b) Substitute: T_cross = (−92.4)/(−0.1989).
Answer: (a) ΔG° = 33.1 kJ mol⁻¹ released; (b) T_cross = 465 K (192 °C).
scenes.caption: ΔG°(298 K) = −33.1 kJ mol⁻¹; T_cross ≈ 465 K.

voiceover.text: Walkthrough three — Haber Gibbs. Delta H is minus ninety-two-point-four, delta S is minus one-ninety-eight-point-nine joules per kelvin per mole. Convert: temperature is two-ninety-eight kelvin, delta S in kilojoules is minus zero-point-one-nine-eight-nine. Substitute: delta G equals minus ninety-two-point-four minus two-ninety-eight times minus zero-point-one-nine-eight-nine. Watch the double negative — that becomes minus ninety-two-point-four plus fifty-nine-point-two-seven, giving minus thirty-three-point-one kilojoules per mole. Negative, so spontaneous at room temperature. Crossover temperature: set delta G to zero — T equals delta H over delta S, both negatives cancel, four hundred and sixty-five kelvin, about one-ninety-two Celsius. This uses the standard-state free-energy change. Actual direction depends on composition through Q. The crossover estimate assumes enthalpy and entropy changes remain approximately constant with temperature; ΔG nought equals zero corresponds to K equals one.

scenes.heading: Three classic IQ3 pitfalls
scenes.body: Students often get these wrong: (1) thinking ΔS is always positive because the Second Law says so, wrong, that's the universe; the system alone can decrease. (2) Setting S° of elements to zero (confusing it with ΔH°f), wrong, S° of every substance is positive. (3) Treating a negative ΔG as a guarantee of fast reaction, wrong, that's thermodynamics, not kinetics. The correct rules: system ΔS can be negative, elements have nonzero S°, spontaneous ≠ fast.
scenes.callout: System ΔS can be negative · elements S° ≠ 0 · spontaneous ≠ fast.
scenes.caption: Three IQ3 traps: always-positive-ΔS, element-S°-zero, spontaneous-means-fast.

voiceover.text: Three classic IQ3 traps. One: students think delta S of the system is always positive because the Second Law says so. Wrong instinct. The correct rule: the Second Law applies to the universe; the system alone can decrease in entropy, as long as the surroundings compensate. Two: students set standard entropy of elements to zero, confusing it with delta H of formation. Wrong instinct. The correct rule: every substance has positive standard entropy — elements included. Three: students treat a negative delta G as a guarantee the reaction will go quickly. Wrong instinct. The correct rule: thermodynamics says it can go; kinetics says how fast. They're independent.

scenes.heading: Boss-fight quick check
scenes.question: For C₂H₄(g) + H₂(g) → C₂H₆(g), ΔH° = −137 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS° = −120.7 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. (a) Predict ΔS sign qualitatively. (b) Calculate ΔG° at 25 °C. (c) Find T_cross.
scenes.pausePrompt: Pause: predict from gas moles, then Gibbs at 298 K, then T_cross = ΔH°/ΔS°.
answerSteps: (a) 2 gas moles → 1 gas mole → ΔS negative (matches the given −120.7).
Convert: T = 298 K, ΔS° = −0.1207 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
(b) ΔG° = −137 − (298 × −0.1207) = −137 + 35.97 = −101 kJ mol⁻¹ → forward-favoured under standard-state conditions.
Answer: (a) ΔS negative; (b) ΔG° = 101 kJ mol⁻¹ released (spontaneous); (c) T_cross ≈ 1135 K.
scenes.caption: ΔS −; ΔG°(298)=−101 kJ mol⁻¹ (spontaneous); T_cross ≈ 1135 K.

voiceover.text: Boss-fight quick check For C₂H₄(g) + H₂(g) → C₂H₆(g), ΔH° = −137 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS° = −120.7 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. (a) Predict ΔS sign qualitatively. (b) Calculate ΔG° at 25 °C. (c) Find T_cross. (a) 2 gas moles → 1 gas mole → ΔS negative (matches the given −120.7). Convert: T = 298 K, ΔS° = −0.1207 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. (b) ΔG° = −137 − (298 × −0.1207) = −137 + 35.97 = −101 kJ mol⁻¹ → forward-favoured under standard-state conditions. Formula: T_cross = ΔH°/ΔS° (set ΔG° = 0). (c) T_cross = (−137) / (−0.1207) = 1135 K (about 862 °C). Answer: (a) ΔS negative; (b) ΔG° = 101 kJ mol⁻¹ released (spontaneous); (c) T_cross ≈ 1135 K.

scenes.heading: IQ3 closing summary
scenes.finalPrompt: Always check: spontaneous means thermodynamically allowed, never automatically fast.
points: Predict ΔS sign qualitatively from gas moles (L11).
Calculate ΔS° = Σ S°(products) − Σ S°(reactants) (L12); elements ≠ 0.
Convert ΔS° from J to kJ before Gibbs.
ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° decides spontaneity; T in kelvin.
scenes.caption: Three skills, one Gibbs equation, one decision rule.

voiceover.text: IQ3 closing summary — and the end of Module four. Five takeaways. One: predict delta S sign qualitatively from gas moles. Two: calculate delta S zero as sum of products minus reactants — and remember, standard entropy of elements is not zero. Three: convert delta S zero from joules to kilojoules before using it in Gibbs. Four: delta G zero equals delta H zero minus T delta S zero decides spontaneity, with T in kelvin. Five: the crossover temperature is delta H over delta S — and remember, spontaneous never automatically means fast. Decision rule: spontaneous is thermodynamically allowed — kinetics is a separate question.
